microbe: a living thing far too small to see
bacteria: tiny single living things found almost everywhere
virus: an even tinier microbe that can cause illness
immune system: the body's built-in defence against microbes
vaccine: something that teaches the body to fight a disease safely
microscope: a tool that makes tiny things look big

Right now, on your hands, in the air, in a single drop of water, there are living things so small that millions could sit on the tip of your finger and you would never know. They are far too tiny for any eye to see. We call them microbes, and they are the most common living things on the whole planet.

image.note: A child's clean-looking hand; a magnified circle over it revealing countless tiny microbes; surprising

pages.text: For most of history, nobody knew they were there. Then someone built a tool that changed everything: the microscope, which makes tiny things look big. Peering through it at a drop of pond water, people were astonished to see it crowded with strange creatures swimming about. A whole hidden world had been discovered.

image.note: An early scientist at a microscope, amazed, a drop of water full of moving specks shown beside

pages.text: There are different kinds of microbe. Bacteria are tiny living things, each just a single blob, that live almost everywhere, in soil, in water, on your skin, and inside you. Then there are viruses, which are far smaller still and stranger, sitting on the very edge of what we call alive. Both are far too small to see.

image.note: A friendly diagram: a rounded bacterium beside a much tinier spiky virus; labelled, non-scary

pages.text: It is tempting to think all these tiny things are nasty and must be scrubbed away. But that would be quite wrong. The great majority of microbes are harmless, and enormous numbers of them are our friends, doing jobs we could not live without. Only a small few ever cause any trouble at all.

image.note: A crowd of cheerful microbes, most smiling, a couple frowning; the balance shown clearly

pages.text: Consider what the helpful microbes do. Inside your own stomach live trillions of good bacteria that help you break down your food. Without them, you could not digest your meals properly. You are not a single creature at all, but a walking community, and most of that community is far too small to see.

image.note: A cutaway of a happy tummy full of tiny helpful bacteria at work; warm, friendly

pages.text: Microbes make food too. Bread rises because tiny living yeast puffs it up. Yoghurt, cheese and many favourite foods are made with the help of friendly bacteria. Out in the world, microbes break down dead leaves and return them to the soil, so new plants can grow. Without them, the whole world would clog up. They are the great recyclers of life.

image.note: Rising bread dough, a pot of yoghurt, and leaves rotting into rich soil; microbes as helpers

chapters.title: The Ones That Make Us Ill

pages.text: Now for the small troublesome few. Some bacteria and viruses can get inside your body and multiply where they are not wanted, and that is what makes you fall ill. A cold, a cough, a tummy upset, these are usually the work of microbes that have slipped in and started to cause damage.

image.note: A child feeling unwell in bed; a gentle inset showing a few troublesome microbes; sympathetic

pages.text: The reason illness can spread is that these microbes are passed from person to person. A cough sends them into the air. Unwashed hands carry them onto food and door handles. Dirty water is full of them. This is not a reason to be frightened, but a reason to be clever, because if we know how they spread, we can stop them.

image.note: Faint microbes travelling from a cough and from an unwashed hand to a shared surface; informative

pages.text: Happily, your body is not helpless. You carry an army inside you, always on guard, called your immune system. When harmful microbes invade, special cells in your blood rush to the attack, surrounding and destroying the invaders. A fever, that hot feeling when you are ill, is often your body deliberately heating up to help this fight.

image.note: Friendly white blood cells surrounding and gobbling up an invading microbe; a battle inside the body

pages.text: Even better, your body remembers. Once it has beaten a particular microbe, it keeps a memory of how to defeat it, so that if the same one ever returns, it is crushed before it can make you ill. This is why you usually catch certain illnesses only once. Your body learned the lesson and never forgot it.

image.note: A "memory cell" holding a wanted poster of a defeated microbe; ready for next time; clever, warm

pages.text: Knowing all this, humans found simple, powerful ways to stay well. Washing your hands with soap sweeps harmful microbes away before they can reach your mouth. Cooking food and boiling water kills the dangerous ones. These plain, everyday habits have saved more lives than almost anything else in history.

image.note: A child washing hands with soap, and a pot of water boiling on a stove; ordinary, powerful

pages.text: Cleverest of all is the vaccine. A vaccine teaches your body to recognise a dangerous microbe safely, before you ever meet the real one, so your inner army is ready and waiting. Thanks to vaccines, terrible diseases that once killed millions of children have become rare or vanished entirely. It is one of humanity's finest inventions.

image.note: A calm, positive clinic scene: a child getting a vaccine, a nurse smiling; brave, reassuring

pages.text: So the hidden world of tiny life is not our enemy. It is mostly our helper, our food-maker, our recycler, and even a part of our own bodies. Only a small few ever mean us harm, and against those we have soap, clean water, cooking and vaccines. We do not need to fear the unseen world. We need to understand it.

image.note: A child confidently going about a normal day, faint friendly microbes all around, unbothered

pages.text: The next time you wash your hands, you will know you are not just following a rule, you are winning a tiny battle. And the next time bread rises or yoghurt sets, you will know that unseen friends did the work. The world is far more crowded, and far more wonderful, than your eyes alone will ever tell you.

image.note: A child holding up a slice of fresh bread, smiling, a warm kitchen; closing, appreciative
